title: What is configuration drift, how do you detect it (`terraform plan`), and how do you reconcile it?
shortTitle: Configuration Drift: What It Is, How to Detect It, and How to Reconcile It

s1_definition.profdef: Configuration drift is the divergence between the real infrastructure and what the Terraform configuration and state describe, caused by changes made outside Terraform, such as a manual console edit, an automated process, or another tool. You detect it by running terraform plan, which refreshes the state against reality and shows any differences as proposed changes, or terraform plan with the refresh-only mode to see drift without proposing fixes. You reconcile it either by re-applying to push reality back to the declared configuration, by updating the configuration to adopt the out-of-band change deliberately, or by importing a resource that exists but is not yet tracked.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India the official blueprint and inventory ledger say the vault door has a specific lock. One night a technician manually swaps the lock without updating the ledger. Now the blueprint and the real vault disagree, which is drift. You find it by walking the branch with the ledger in hand and comparing, which is what plan does. You fix it either by restoring the lock the blueprint specifies, or by formally updating the blueprint to accept the new lock, or by adding a newly installed safe that nobody recorded into the ledger so future audits know about it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Drift is reality diverging from the declared configuration due to out-of-band changes; detect it with terraform plan and reconcile by re-applying, updating the config to match, or importing untracked resources.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Configuration drift is the divergence between the real infrastructure and what the Terraform configuration and state describe, caused by changes made outside Terraform, such as a manual console edit, an automated process, or another tool. You detect it by running terraform plan, which refreshes the state against reality and shows any differences as proposed changes, or terraform plan with the refresh-only mode to see drift without proposing fixes. You reconcile it either by re-applying to push reality back to the declared configuration, by updating the configuration to adopt the out-of-band change deliberately, or by importing a resource that exists but is not yet tracked.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India the official blueprint and inventory ledger say the vault door has a specific lock. One night a technician manually swaps the lock without updating the ledger. Now the blueprint and the real vault disagree, which is drift. You find it by walking the branch with the ledger in hand and comparing, which is what plan does. You fix it either by restoring the lock the blueprint specifies, or by formally updating the blueprint to accept the new lock, or by adding a newly installed safe that nobody recorded into the ledger so future audits know about it.

**One line to remember:** Drift is reality diverging from the declared configuration due to out-of-band changes; detect it with terraform plan and reconcile by re-applying, updating the config to match, or importing untracked resources.

sections.s2_technical:
Drift happens because Terraform is not the only actor that can change cloud resources. An engineer might open the AWS console and bump a database instance class during an incident, an auto-scaling process might change a setting, another team's tool might edit a security group, or a cloud provider might alter a default. Any of these makes the real resource differ from what Terraform's state and configuration say, and because Terraform plans by diffing desired configuration against state against reality, drift directly affects the next plan.

Detection starts with terraform plan. Plan first refreshes: it queries the providers for the current real attributes and compares them to the state. If reality differs from the configuration, plan shows changes that would bring reality back in line, which surfaces the drift as a set of proposed updates. To inspect drift without any intent to change, I use plan in refresh-only mode, which reports what changed in reality relative to state so I can decide deliberately, and I can also run a refresh-only apply to update the state to match reality without touching resources. In mature setups I run a scheduled plan in CI, often called drift detection, that alerts the team when the real world no longer matches the declared configuration, so drift is caught proactively rather than discovered during the next change.

Reconciliation has three distinct strategies and choosing correctly matters. The first is to re-apply the existing configuration, which pushes reality back to what the code declares, effectively reverting the manual change. This is the right choice when the out-of-band change was unintended or unauthorized, because the configuration is the source of truth and should win. The second is to update the configuration to match the new reality, which is the right choice when the manual change was actually desirable, for example an emergency scale-up during an incident that should be made permanent, so I codify it and apply so state and code agree. The third is terraform import, used when a resource exists in the cloud but is not in the state at all, which is a form of drift where Terraform is simply unaware of a resource; import brings it under management so future plans account for it. A refresh-only apply is a fourth, narrower tool to realign state with reality without changing either resources or configuration.

The senior discipline is preventive and procedural. I minimize drift by forbidding manual console changes to Terraform-managed resources, routing all changes through code and the pipeline, and using guardrails like IAM policies that restrict who can modify managed resources directly. I run scheduled drift detection so surprises are caught early. And when drift does occur, I make a conscious decision per resource whether the code should win or reality should win, rather than blindly applying, because in a bank blindly reverting an emergency fix or blindly adopting an unauthorized change can both be dangerous. Drift handling is as much about process and intent as it is about the plan command.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India our ledger database and security groups are Terraform-managed, and drift bit us in two instructive ways.

Problem 1 — during a late-night incident an on-call engineer manually bumped the ledger database instance class in the console to handle load and did not tell anyone. The next Terraform plan showed it wanted to shrink the database back, which would have hurt production. This is exactly the decision point: revert via re-apply, or adopt the change in code.

Problem 2 — another team created a security group rule directly in the console that Terraform did not know about, so it was untracked drift. The fix was to import it so it became managed. This is exactly the import scenario.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `CloudReality` holding actual resource attributes, a `TerraformState` holding the declared values, a `DriftDetector` that diffs them like terraform plan, and a `Reconciler` that applies one of the three strategies. We detect the database drift and the untracked security group, decide per resource, and then run a transfer for Rajesh and Priya on the correctly reconciled database.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the drift simulation
javac -d out sim/src/main/java/com/bank/drift/*.java
java -cp out com.bank.drift.DriftDemo

# Real Terraform drift workflow
terraform plan                          # shows drift as proposed changes
terraform plan -refresh-only            # see drift WITHOUT proposing fixes
terraform apply -refresh-only           # realign STATE to reality (no resource change)
terraform apply                         # re-apply: push reality back to code (code wins)
terraform import aws_security_group_rule.ledger_allow sgr-0123  # adopt untracked resource
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a ledger database whose class is changed out of band, and an untracked security group rule.

Step 1 — Initially the declared class and the real class of the ledger database both read db.m5.large, so a plan shows no drift.

Step 2 — During an incident someone manually bumps the real class to db.m5.2xlarge without changing the code. The next plan refreshes reality against state and reports drift: declared is large but actual is 2xlarge.

Step 3 — We make a deliberate decision. Because the larger class is genuinely needed, we choose to adopt reality into the configuration rather than revert it, codifying the emergency change. A follow-up plan now shows no drift because code and reality agree.

Step 4 — Separately, a security group rule was created directly in the console. A plan finds it exists in the cloud but is not tracked by Terraform, flagging it as a candidate for import. We run import so the rule becomes managed and future plans account for it.

Step 5 — With the database class correctly reconciled and the rule now tracked, a transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya runs on the ledger database successfully, tying the reconciled infrastructure to a working operation.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Configuration drift is when the real infrastructure diverges from what my Terraform configuration and state describe, and it happens because Terraform is not the only thing that can change cloud resources. An engineer might edit a setting in the console during an incident, an auto-scaling process might change something, another team's tool might touch a security group, or a provider default might shift. Since Terraform plans by diffing the desired configuration against state against reality, any of these out-of-band changes directly shows up the next time I plan.

I detect drift with terraform plan, which refreshes by querying the providers for the real attributes and comparing them to state, then surfaces any divergence as proposed changes. When I want to inspect drift without any intent to change anything, I use the refresh-only plan, which reports what moved in reality relative to state, and a refresh-only apply to realign state to reality without touching resources. In mature setups I run a scheduled drift-detection plan in CI that alerts the team the moment reality stops matching the declared configuration, so drift is caught proactively instead of discovered during the next change.

Reconciliation has three strategies and choosing correctly is the real skill. I can re-apply the existing configuration, which pushes reality back to what the code declares and effectively reverts an unintended change, which is right when the code should remain the source of truth. I can update the configuration to match the new reality, which is right when the out-of-band change was actually desirable, such as an emergency scale-up I want to make permanent, so I codify it and apply so code and state agree. Or I can use terraform import when a resource exists in the cloud but is not tracked at all, bringing it under management so future plans account for it.

In my project at the National Bank of India both cases happened. During a late-night incident an on-call engineer manually bumped our ledger database instance class and did not update the code, so the next plan wanted to shrink it back, which would have hurt production. Because the larger class was genuinely needed, we adopted the change into the configuration rather than reverting it. Separately, a security group rule was created directly in the console and was untracked, so we imported it to bring it under management. The broader discipline I apply is preventive: forbid manual edits to Terraform-managed resources, route every change through the pipeline, run scheduled drift detection, and when drift does occur decide consciously per resource whether the code should win or reality should win, because in a bank blindly reverting an emergency fix or blindly adopting an unauthorized change are both dangerous.
